incident_spec.summary: MySQL issue-search query is slow because a leading-wildcard, case-insensitive subject filter is evaluated together with OR-heavy project ACL logic and dependent membership/module checks, forcing a large scan of `issues` before `LIMIT 10` can short-circuit.
symptoms: Application performance is poor under up to 100 concurrent users.
The slowest query reportedly takes about 15 seconds.
EXPLAIN shows a large estimated row scan on `issues` and dependent subqueries on `members` and `enabled_modules`.
The query returns at most 10 rows but still examines a large portion of the issue table.
incident_spec.mechanism: The optimizer cannot make the `LOWER(issues.subject) LIKE LOWER('%255392%')` predicate selective via index access, so it must evaluate many candidate `issues` rows while applying ACL predicates that expand through multiple OR branches and correlated membership/module checks. With `ORDER BY issues.id DESC LIMIT 10`, MySQL can still need to walk a large part of the primary-key order before finding enough qualifying rows.

facts.evidence: Tabular Explain shows PRIMARY on issues plus DEPENDENT SUBQUERY on members and enabled_modules
Leading wildcard LIKE with LOWER() is not index-friendly; dependent subqueries and OR branches increase per-row evaluation cost.

assumptions: The reported slow query is representative of the main bottleneck and not merely one pathological execution.
The production schema has no highly selective functional index that would make the `LOWER(subject) LIKE '%...%'` predicate cheap.
The relevant MySQL version behaves similarly to the examined environment for dependent subqueries and ORDER BY ... LIMIT planning.
Synthetic data can approximate the fanout and skew well enough to reproduce the slowdown mechanism even if not the exact production plan.
unknowns: Exact MySQL version and optimizer settings.
Whether additional indexes exist on the production `issues`, `projects`, or ACL tables beyond the partial schema shown.
Exact distribution of the search token across `issues.subject` values.
Whether the 15-second runtime was observed cold, warm, or under concurrent load.
Whether `custom_values` contributes indirectly elsewhere in the application but not in this specific query path.

feasibility.rationale: The exact production accident cannot be reproduced because the original data and full schema are unavailable, but the core mechanism is reproducible: a large `issues` table, sparse matching subjects, public/private ACL skew, dependent membership/module lookups, and the same query shape are sufficient to recreate the expensive scan behavior.
missing_capabilities: Exact MySQL optimizer settings from the incident time
unmatched_conditions: Exact subject/token placement in production rows is unknown
Exact ACL membership pattern for user IDs 44 and 638 is unknown
Exact runtime under concurrent application traffic is unknown

value_skew.issues.subject: A very rare token '255392' appears in about 1/30000 rows and is concentrated near high issue ids.
value_skew.issues.project_id: Most issues map to a few hot projects; a small set of ACL-visible projects is overrepresented among matching rows.
value_skew.members.user_id: Membership rows are concentrated on user IDs 44 and 638 only.
value_skew.projects.is_public: Most projects are public, but a meaningful minority are private.
value_skew.projects.status: Most projects are active; a minority have status 9.

predicate_selectivity.projects.status <> 9: High selectivity but not enough to avoid a scan
predicate_selectivity.enabled_modules.name = 'issue_tracking': High selectivity only if enabled_modules is sparse

join_selectivity.issues.project_id -> projects.id: Many-to-one from issues to projects, preserving large fanout
join_selectivity.enabled_modules.project_id -> projects.i: One module row per active project
join_selectivity.members.project_id -> projects.id: Sparse membership rows per project with focused user IDs

validation_criteria: The synthetic schema loads successfully in a dedicated test database.
The target query returns a small result set while still requiring a large scan over `issues`.
EXPLAIN evidence shows the ACL subqueries are evaluated per candidate row rather than fully precomputed away.

The OR-heavy ACL logic and dependent subqueries prevent early pruning of most rows.
